doc.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Reflections on judging and writing songs
summary: Moore says he cannot judge his own songs, cites Jerome Kern, and regrets not writing daily.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: That’s interesting. The opposite may happen sometime. You may write something that you just think is the best —

Oh that has happened. That’s happened more often than the other way around. You kind of say wow. And then you give it to somebody and they say, “That’s nice,” you know. And so I mean I don’t know whether we ever really know or can tell, or whether I can, other people can I’m sure. But you wonder if — Jerome Kern when he finished “All The Things You Are” said I’ve just written a classic. This is going to be the greatest, one of the great songs ever, and it’s perfect. Or whether he just thought well I did that one today, and I’ve got four more to do.

You wonder if they, how jazz musicians, why they’ve chosen certain songs to latch on to like that. I mean it seems to be perfect for improvising and the whole thing, but like you said, he may have had no idea that that was going to happen with that particular tune.

Somebody said to me one time, a tune has a life of its own. It’s like you’re giving birth to a child and you send it out into the world, and you don’t know what’s going to happen to it or where it’s going to go. I really kind of kick myself for not doing more writing, because the more you do it the better — it’s like anything else — the more you do it the better at it you get. And to be disciplined enough to sit down every day and say okay I’m going to write for two hours, and whatever comes out comes out. And just kind of let it alone and not re-work it and not go over it and over it again. Just see what happens. Wonderful things happen when you just go to that well every day. And I don’t do it enough. I’m a compulsive practicing person. I practice a lot. I don’t call it practicing though, I say playing. But I’m not compulsive about anything else. That and pasta.
